annotationRationale: Fractional exponents reduce the identity to an integer equation, and bounds determine the indices completely. Divisor enumeration is another finish to the same route, so it is not presented as a separate method. No assumption is made that the unreduced numerator and denominator must individually equal 25 and 36.

classificationReview.areaCheck: Number Theory is defensible because integer restrictions and completeness determine the answer, although the reduction uses algebra. No obvious subject repair is needed.

review.questionCheck: For the current domain N>1, radical conversion and equality of exponents are valid. The integer bounds force (a,b,c)=(2,3,6), so choice B is correct. The archived AoPS stem says N≠1 rather than N>1; the candidate correctly uses the current domain. There is no current stem, choice or figure contradiction.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: The LIVE divisor finish and AoPS Solution 1 share the retained exponent-reduction route; the candidate's second bound supplies a complete uniqueness argument. Divisor enumeration would be another finish rather than a beneficial separate method. AoPS Solutions 2 and 3 make unjustified numerator-denominator identifications, and Solution 4 uses unsupported factor restrictions, so those arguments should remain omitted. No shared-bank methods were supplied.
review.annotationCheck: Fractional exponents and complete integer-equation reasoning are suitable assessed concepts. Exponent operations support the reduction, and integer solutions of inequalities precisely describe the bounding steps.
review.areaCheck: Number Theory is defensible because integer restrictions and completeness determine the answer, although the reduction uses algebra. No obvious subject repair is needed.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The exponent is 1/a+1/(ab)+1/(abc). The upper bound gives a≤63/25, hence a=2. Then 1<7b/18≤3/2 yields 18/7<b≤27/7, whose only integer is 3. This forces c=6, and the final substitution verifies existence as well as uniqueness.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: The cited LIVE explanation and AoPS Solution 1 support the exponent reduction and bound on a. The candidate honestly identifies its added tight bound on b, avoids the flawed denominator assumptions elsewhere in AoPS, and uses original exposition with the proper third-party basis.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The reason for changing radicals into powers is clear. Positivity, integrality, strict and weak endpoints, and the final existence check are all explained sufficiently.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: Fractional exponents cover the radical conversion; h040 supplies the supporting exponent-law pattern. h020 and integer-diophantine-equations directly cover the finite integer bounds and completeness.
